extracted.intended_audience: zoologists, taxonomists, museum curators, and field collectors working on freshwater sponges, hydroids, and polyzoa (India/Burma region)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for delimiting species, subspecies, varieties, and phases; rules and practical recommendations for designation and treatment of type specimens; and conventions for nomenclatural practice in a faunal monograph of freshwater sponges, hydroids, and polyzoa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of individuals differing in constant characters of a definite nature and of systematic importance from all others in the same genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What characters are of systematic importance may differ for different groups (footnote). This definition is to be used when estimating the value of 'species' in the volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subspecies definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An isolated or local race, the individuals of which differ from others included in the same species in characters that are constant but either somewhat indefinite or else of little systematic importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on geographic isolation and differences that are constant but of lesser or indefinite systematic importance compared to full species-level differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of individuals not isolated geographically from others of the same species but nevertheless exhibiting slight, not altogether constant, or indefinite differences from the typical form of the species (i.e., the form first described).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Varieties are not geographically isolated from the typical form; differences may be slight or not altogether constant. Use of 'variety' signals limited or inconsistent distinction from the type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A peculiar form assumed by the individuals of a species which are exposed to peculiarities in environment and differ from normal individuals as a direct result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phases are environmentally induced forms; differences are a direct result of peculiar environment rather than hereditary systematic characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for uncertain forms (variety vs subspecies)
rubrics_metrics.description: When imperfection of information renders it difficult or impossible to distinguish between a variety and a subspecies, it is best to call the form a variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calling an uncertain form a variety is conservative: the term does not imply special knowledge about distribution or environmental conditions and avoids over-committing to subspecific status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type-specimen practice and schools of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Two schools exist: (1) one specimen only must be the type of a species; (2) acceptance of several specimens as types (paratypes). Theoretical objections exist to a single specimen being the 'ideal' type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Museum rules often force selection of a single type; many workers adopt a single type with co-types or paratypes. The author prefers regarding the whole original material as the basis of the species but concedes practical need to pick a single specimen as the type, the remainder being called co-types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling types for compound or fragmentable organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: For organisms that are compound (colonial hydroids, sponges that break into fragments), selecting one particular individual or piece as the type is problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If forced to select a single piece, one may pick the biggest piece as the type and designate smaller pieces as 'schizotype'. Practical advice acknowledges that no one piece is inherently sacrosanct; terms like 'schizotype' can be used for fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and technical type-terms (topotype, genotype, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms such as topotype, genotype, et hujus generis omnis are highly technical and form a specialized terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The finer distinctions and definitions of these special type-terms are a technical industry and are not discussed in detail in this volume; practitioners should consult specialized references when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclatural standard-setting (choice of authorities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt recent comprehensive monographs as practical standards for nomenclature rather than unearthing obsolete names: e.g., for Spongillidæ use Potts (1887) as baseline; for freshwater polyzoa follow Allman (1856); for other polyzoa follow Hincks (1880) insofar as recent research permits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author avoids elaborate synonymy of species described earlier than these works as a waste of time given difficulty of precise definitions and scarcity of early types. Works not available locally are marked with an asterisk; preference is to cite works consultable in local libraries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical documentation of material and provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: List the location (institutional collection) where types, co-types, schizotypes and other material are preserved, and document which specimens were examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The volume lists types preserved in various museums and notes when types are 'not in existence' or when institutions failed to confirm preservation. Include bracketed notation for species not yet found in fresh water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for rejecting wind/marine-current dispersal explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference about origin/dispersal of freshwater sponges and polyzoa should consider the morphology and resting reproductive bodies: many characteristic genera have resting bodies fixed to solid objects or lack apparatus for becoming light; gemmules/statoblasts may be unusually heavy and adhesive; some statoblasts lack air-cells that would make them float.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many resting bodies are heavy and adhere firmly, aerial or marine current transport is unlikely as an explanation for the peculiar Malabar fauna; therefore prefer geological/biogeographical explanations (e.g., former land connections) in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of geological/biogeographical evidence for faunal relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: When taxonomic distributions show affinities between regions (Malabar, Africa, East Indies), prefer seeking geographical or geological explanations (e.g., former land-connections) rather than invoking long-distance passive transport when biological traits contradict transport feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: similarity of genera/subgenera across Malabar and Africa, and traits of resting bodies, make a former land connection (probably late Cretaceous when Western Ghats higher) a more satisfactory hypothesis than wind or marine transport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-collection habitat assessment for sponges/polyzoa
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of ponds/tanks that make them good collecting grounds include: presence of solid objects for attachment, prolific aquatic vegetation (Pistia, Lemna, Limnanthemum), brickwork or artificial stonework at sides, sufficient depth, and favourable light and shade; ponds lacking such features are poor in sponges and polyzoa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples: Calcutta 'tanks' with abundant weeds and solid supports (e.g., Indian Museum tank) yield many species; tanks lacking solid objects and vegetation are poor. Temporary shallow pools and very turbid or strongly tidal waters may not be productive for certain groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in asserting restricted distribution from limited records
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assert that a species' apparent restriction to a small area is real when knowledge of representatives in surrounding regions is poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: some brackish-water species known only from the Ganges delta may appear restricted, but this may be due to ignorance of Indian representatives; avoid over-interpreting sparse records as true endemism.
